items.notes: A 10 W panel (about 14 V open-circuit) in direct sun powered the board and charged a lithium-ion cell at up to 5.3 W, with the charger die at about 32 C. A 6 W panel in shade was reported as an "Unqualified adapter" and did not charge. The charger checks the source when it first connects, so a weak panel can fail that check.

items.feature: Source selection between USB-C and DC
items.notes: With a USB wall charger (5.1 V) and a solar panel (13.5 V) both connected, the board ran from either input and the host could switch between them in either direction. Force Solar stayed on solar with USB valid, and Off cut both. Which input the charger picks by itself when both appear at the same moment was not tested; the datasheet gives USB (port 1) priority. A battery bank is a poor test source: it switches its output off at low load and the charger then sees about 2.3 V.
With `DIS_ACDRV` set, the gate drive between `ACDRV1_NODE` and `MUX1_MID` fell from about 5.5 V to about 0 V, `VBUS` lost its 5 V and charging stopped. Clearing it brought the input back.

On a 6 W panel in dim, changing light the charger started charging once the panel could supply it and kept charging as the light varied. The panel voltage follows the MPPT ratio (about 9.3 to 10 V at 0.8125, 10.2 to 11 V at 0.875). The two ratios have not been compared for power: the light changed too much to tell them apart.
Reached fast charge from USB at about 470 mA with no thermistor fitted and `ts_ignore: true` set. Without that setting the charger suspends charging by default.
Works. It blinks while charging is suspended. Too bright, so the series resistor was raised in the current design (untested).

items.feature: Charger and input readings in Home Assistant
items.notes: Input source, input voltage and fault status.

On the prototype the protection FETs were mounted the wrong way round, so their body diodes would conduct on a reversed input. The current design turns them around. Do not connect a reversed supply to the prototype.
Toggling it from Home Assistant powers the STEMMA QT port's device on and off.
Works on battery power alone. With USB connected it does nothing, as the charger ignores it while an adapter is present. A brief tap of `SW3` does not wake the board; holding it does.

items.feature: `SW3` held about 10 s to hard power-cycle
items.notes: The board dropped off the API and reconnected.
Board keeps running with USB unplugged.

Charging stopped with "Charge terminated" at about 4.19 V, "Battery Fully Charged" turned on, and the gauge reported 100%. A LiFePO4 cell also finished with "Charge terminated", after reaching its 3.65 V limit.

Set to 180 mA, the battery charged at 178 mA. Raising it to 1050 mA raised the charge current well above that. On a LiFePO4 cell, limits of 500, 1000 and 1500 mA gave about 463, 1035 and 1552 mA into the cell. At 2000 mA the cell reached its 3.65 V limit and the current tapered from about 1.7 A. The charger die reached 37.5 C with no thermal regulation and no fault.
Setting "Input Current Limit" to 210 mA from Home Assistant lowered the battery current while charging.

With the USB cable unplugged and the board running from a 4.15 V Li-ion cell, pressing "Charger Shutdown" over WiFi took the board off the network within seconds. Plugging USB back in woke it, and it answered a ping about 8 s later with its settings intact.
"Charger Temperature" read 16 to 38 C while charging at up to 1.7 A.
The charger reduces its current when it gets hot. It did not trigger in the tests so far.
With it on, the input current fell from about 430 mA to about 30 mA, charging stopped and the board ran on the battery. The input FETs stay on; only the converter stops.
Turning "Enable Charger Status LED" off turns the LED dark.
Charging carried on without a break, and the charge current limit and input selection were unchanged. The charge voltage limit and the ship-FET setting were not read back.
"Charger Interrupt" fires when USB is plugged or unplugged.
With a battery connected, after a driver fix for the state-of-charge reading.
The gauge blocked the internal I2C bus. The `FG_PWR` jumper now defaults to powering it from the system rail.
Added in the current design.
With a thermistor fitted it reads sensibly (25.0 C, against 25.4 C from the charger). Without one it reads implausibly cold, so a thermistor has to be fitted.
Run the current and board offset calibrations with the pack at rest, and compare the gauge's battery current with the charger's.
With thermistors fitted the charger reads 25.4 C and the gauge 25.0 C, within half a degree of each other, and the gauge no longer reports "Charge inhibited".

items.feature: Charging with the thermistor check on (`ts_ignore` off)
items.notes: With thermistors taped to the cell, charging started with `ts_ignore` off and ran without a fault or a "Charge inhibited" message. Stopping at the end of charge has not been checked with the thermistor check on.

items.feature: `FG_ALERT` input and wake from deep sleep
items.notes: The "Fuel Gauge Alert" input follows the pin, and pulling `FG_ALERT` low woke the board from deep sleep (an ext1 wake on GPIO4). The pin was grounded by hand; the gauge was not the source.

With low and critical charge selected in `alert_configuration`, the "Fuel Gauge Alert" input went on while the gauge reported low and critical charge, on two boards. The gauge ships with that register at 0 and never asserts the pin until it is written, so the option must be set. Releasing the pin with "Clear Fuel Gauge Alert" has not been checked.

items.feature: Wi-Fi range on the external antenna
items.notes: With the external antenna fitted, two boards near the access point read -44 and -49 dBm. A third, through several walls, reads about -73 dBm on 2.4 GHz and drops its connection now and then. Forcing 2.4 GHz did not change the signal.
